The Fed Just Raised Rates. What It Means for Your Money

2026-11-02

Subscribe for one money story a week

About this video

On September 17, 2026, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in more than three years. Here's exactly what that means for your credit card, your mortgage, your car loan and your savings. Penny the coin explains the Fed's 2026 rate hike with real data: what the Fed actually controls, the rate rollercoaster since 2022, why an oil shock pushed the Fed to act, the split October vote, what happens to credit card rates (now over 21%), mortgages and car loans, why the average savings account still pays almost nothing, a simple rate-hike checklist, and what could happen next. 0:00 Intro: the first hike since 2023 0:23 What the Fed actually controls 1:03 The rollercoaster since 2022 1:34 Why raise rates now? 2:19 Why not just keep rates low? 2:49 A split decision 3:24 Does this change your payment? 3:45 Your credit card 4:37 Mortgages and car loans 5:31 Your savings 6:25 Your rate-hike checklist 6:57 What happens next? 7:26 Recap Data: Fed funds target range (DFEDTARU, DFEDTARL), bank prime loan rate (DPRIME), credit card plan rates (TERMCBCCALLNS) and 48-month new car loan rates (TERMCBAUTO48NS) from the Federal Reserve; 30-year mortgage rate (Freddie Mac, MORTGAGE30US); national savings rate (FDIC, SNDR); CPI and unemployment (BLS); retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, through October 2026. Transcript

On September 17, the Federal Reserve did something it hadn't done in more than three years. It raised interest rates. Then in October, it held them there, and two officials voted to raise them again. If you have a credit card, a car loan, a mortgage, or even just a savings account, this affects you. Here's exactly how. First, what does the Fed actually control? It's not your mortgage rate, and it's not your credit card rate. At least, not directly. It sets a target for the federal funds rate. That's the interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. Right now, that target is 3.75% to 4%. When banks pay more to borrow, they charge you more to borrow. That's how one number ripples through the whole economy. Congress gave the Fed two jobs: keep prices stable, and keep as many people working as possible. Economists call it the dual mandate, and those two jobs sometimes pull in opposite directions. Here's where that rate has been over the last ten years. In early 2022, it was close to zero. Then inflation took off, and the Fed raised rates 11 times in about a year and a half, up to 5.5%. Once inflation cooled, it started cutting, in 2024 and 2025, down to a range of 3.5% to 3.75%. Then, in September 2026, it turned around and raised rates again. So why now? In one word: oil. After the war with Iran stopped tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, gas and diesel prices soared. We broke that down in our last video. Inflation climbed from about 2.4% in February to 3.7% in September, almost double the Fed's 2% target. The Fed's job is to keep prices stable, and its main tool is interest rates. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive, so people and businesses spend a little less, and that cools prices down. But there's a catch. The Fed can't pump more oil, and higher rates can't reopen a shipping lane. They can only slow spending, so a fuel shock doesn't turn into higher prices for everything. You might wonder: why doesn't the Fed just keep rates low and make life easier? Because if inflation gets stuck, everyone's paycheck buys a little less every single year. That's what happened in the 1970s. Inflation hit about 15% in 1980, and the Fed had to push this rate to about 19% in 1981 to break it, which helped cause a deep recession. Small, early steps today are meant to avoid ever needing medicine that strong again. At its meeting on October 28, the Fed held rates steady. But the vote was 10 to 2, and both officials who disagreed wanted another hike. Twelve people vote on rates: the seven Fed governors in Washington, the president of the New York Fed, and four of the other regional Fed presidents, who take turns. That shows the debate inside the Fed right now. Some worry inflation is getting stuck. Others worry about slowing the economy too much. So far, the job market is holding up. Unemployment was 4.2% in September. Before we go through your bills, one important point. If your mortgage or car loan has a fixed rate, this hike doesn't change your payment at all. It matters for new loans, and for anything with a variable rate: credit cards, home equity lines of credit, and adjustable rate mortgages. Those can go up within a month or two. Now, what does this mean for you? Let's start with the most expensive debt most people have: credit cards. Most credit cards have variable rates tied to the prime rate, which moves almost one for one with the Fed. The prime rate is now 7%, and the average interest rate on credit card accounts at banks is about 21.2%. If you carry a $5,000 balance at that rate, you'd pay about $1,060 a year in interest. This hike itself added a quarter of a percentage point. On that same $5,000, that's only about $12.50 more a year. The real problem is the 21% itself. That's why paying down card debt is one of the best guaranteed returns you can get. Every dollar you pay off stops costing you over 21% a year. Mortgage rates don't follow the Fed directly. They follow what investors expect for inflation and interest rates over the next several years. In late February, the 30 year mortgage rate was about 5.98%. As oil and inflation jumped, it climbed as high as 7.4% in October. This week, it's about 7.24%. On a $300,000 loan, that's the difference between about $1,795 and $2,044 a month, or about $2,996 more every year. Higher rates also keep many homeowners from selling, because they don't want to give up the low rate they already have. That means fewer homes for sale. Car loans are pricier too. The average rate on a four year new car loan from a bank is about 7.47%. Higher rates do have a bright side. Savers can earn more, but only if they go looking. According to the FDIC, the national average rate on savings accounts is just 0.38%. With inflation at 3.7%, money sitting there loses about 3.3% of its buying power every year. Many online banks pay savings rates much closer to the Fed's rate. As long as the bank is FDIC insured, your deposits are protected up to $250,000. On a $10,000 emergency fund, 0.38% earns you about $38 a year. An account paying 3.5% would earn about $350. And if you won't need some money for a while, a certificate of deposit, or CD, can lock in today's higher rate for months or even years. So here's a simple checklist. One: pay down variable rate debt first, starting with whatever charges the highest rate. Two: if you carry a card balance, call your card company and ask for a lower rate. It works more often than you'd think. Three: make sure your savings are actually earning something. And four: if you're buying a home or a car, compare at least three lenders. A small difference in rate can add up to thousands of dollars. And five: don't panic. Rates move slowly, and you have time to make a plan. So, will the Fed raise rates again? It mostly depends on oil. If shipping through Hormuz recovers and energy prices fall, inflation could cool, and the Fed may not need to hike again. If oil stays above $100 and higher prices keep spreading, more hikes are possible. Watch the monthly inflation report. If energy prices keep easing, that's a sign the pressure is fading. The Fed meets again in December, and we'll break it down when it does. So the Fed raised rates to fight inflation caused by an oil shock. It can't fix the oil, but it can make borrowing more expensive, and that touches almost every part of your financial life. Pay down expensive debt, make your savings work for you, and compare before you borrow. Next time: how banks create money out of thin air. Subscribe to Coin Theory so you don't miss it.
